y-m-15-01.title: If the average is 12 books, must there be a day with 12 books borrowed?
y-m-15-01.topic: Meaning of the average: the average and the actual records
y-m-15-01.goal: Make a case where no record equals the average, to correct the idea that 'the average is one of the actual records' with a counterexample, and say what the average tells and does not tell.
y-m-15-01.material: At Starlight Library, the number of books borrowed each day was recorded for 4 days, Monday to Thursday. The average of the 4 days was 12 books. The number of books borrowed in a day is a natural number from 0 to 30. Seoyun said, “The average is 12 books, so on at least one of the 4 days, exactly 12 books must have been borrowed.”
y-m-15-01.thinking.0: Testing a claim that 'it must be so' with a single counterexample
y-m-15-01.thinking.1: Making different records that satisfy a condition (the total)
y-m-15-01.thinking.2: Telling what the average tells from what it does not tell
y-m-15-01.prereq.0: Meaning of the average: the value when all the data is made even (5th-grade level)
y-m-15-01.prereq.1: Finding the sum of four numbers
y-m-15-01.s.s1.prompt: What is the surest way to find out whether Seoyun's 'must be so' is right?
y-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.0: Underline the word 'must' in Seoyun's statement, and think about what kind of example is needed to break it.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.1: First decide what the total of the books on the four days must be for the average to be 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.a: Find many records with an average of 12 books and see whether they include a day with 12 books
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.a: Many examples fitting does not prove 'must'. 'Must' can be broken by even one opposite example.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.b: Ask the librarian whether there was a day among the 4 with 12 books borrowed
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.b: You would only learn about these 4 days of records. You would not be testing the statement 'if the average is 12 books it must be so' itself.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.c: Try to make a record with an average of 12 books in which there is no day with 12 books
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.c: This tests the word 'must' directly. All you need is to make an example that keeps the condition but goes against the statement.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.d: Check once more how to find an average
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.d: Knowing how to calculate is different from testing whether 'it must be so' is right.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.explain: The statement 'it must be so' becomes false with even one record that keeps the condition but is not so. So the surest way is to make a record with an average of 12 books and no day with 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different records with an average of 12 books and no day on which exactly 12 books were borrowed. (Monday m, Tuesday t, Wednesday w, Thursday h) Records that only swap the days count as the same record.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what happens when there are days above 12 and days below 12. If one day is 2 below 12, by how much must another day go up?
y-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.1: First make a pair like (11, 13), then fit the sum for the other two days.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All are natural numbers from 0 to 30.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of books in a day must be a natural number from 0 to 30.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The average of the 4 days is 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The average of the 4 days is not 12 books. Check the sum of the four numbers.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c3: There is no day with 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c3: There is a day when 12 books were borrowed. Change the number of books on that day.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.explain: For example, (10, 11, 13, 14) has a sum of 48 books, so the average is 12 books, but there is no day with 12 books. (8, 9, 15, 16) and (0, 30, 9, 9) work too. The average does not have to be one of the actual records.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.prompt: What will you say to Seoyun? Explain using the numbers of the record you just made.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.0: You may take one of the records you made in the step above as it is.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write in one sentence 'in what way Seoyun's statement is wrong', and then add a numerical example.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. That's not necessarily so. For example, ...
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check again that the four numbers in your record add up to 48?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write it so that the point 'there is no day with 12' can be seen in the numbers?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write, even in a few words, what the average tells (the value when everything is made even)?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.model.0: That's not necessarily so. For example, with 10, 11, 13, and 14 books, the sum is 48 books, so the average is 12 books, but there is not a single day with 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.model.1: You're wrong. 0, 30, 9, and 9 books also have an average of 12 books, but there is no day with 12. The average is the value when everything is made even, so it can be different from the actual records.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: I gave an extreme example. I connected it to the meaning of the average.

y-m-15-02.title: If the average changes after the sixth test
y-m-15-02.topic: Finding one more average from an average: an average you already know and new data
y-m-15-02.goal: Find and fix the error that arises when combining an already-known average with newly obtained data to work out a new average, and find several new scores that match a target average.
y-m-15-02.material: Hajun took the math unit test five times, and the average of his scores is 70 points. All the scores are natural numbers from 0 to 100. On the sixth unit test he got 90 points. Hajun said, “Now let's find the average of the six tests,” and solved it as below.
y-m-15-02.thinking.0: Finding the line that has an error in the solution
y-m-15-02.thinking.1: Questioning 'how many data values the average represents'
y-m-15-02.thinking.2: Making several new data values that keep a target average
y-m-15-02.prereq.0: Meaning of the average (sum ÷ number) and going back from an average to the sum (5th-grade level)
y-m-15-02.prereq.1: Addition and division with three-digit numbers
y-m-15-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that is wrong in Hajun's solution. (Count the lines starting from 1.)
y-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.0: In line 3, look at how many scores the 70 stands for.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think backwards about what the total of the five scores is, and compare it with the 80 points in line 3.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.line.0: The average of the scores from the five tests was 70 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.line.2: The average of the six tests is (70 + 90) ÷ 2 = 80 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.line.3: The sixth score is higher than 70 points, so the average of the six tests goes above 70 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The 70 points is not one score but a value that evens out the scores of five tests. So the problem is that 70 points and 90 points were each counted only once. The sum of the five tests is 70×5=350 points, and adding 90 points gives 440 points; dividing by 6 gives about 73.3 points. The statement 'the average goes up' in line 4 is right.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.prompt: After taking the seventh test, the average of the seven tests became exactly 75 points. Find 3 different possible pairs of the sixth score s and the seventh score u. (Both scores are natural numbers from 0 to 100, and the sixth was lower than the seventh.)
y-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.0: For the average of the seven tests to be 75 points, what must the total of the seven scores be?
y-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract the sum of the five tests to find the sum of the remaining two scores, then fix one score and fit the other.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Both scores are natural numbers from 0 to 100.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The scores must be natural numbers from 0 to 100 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The average of the seven tests is 75 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The average of the seven tests is not 75 points. Think again starting from the sum of the five tests.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The sixth is lower than the seventh.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The sixth score must be lower than the seventh.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.explain: The sum of the seven is 75×7=525 points and the sum of the first five is 350 points, so the sum of the two scores is 175 points. Pairs with sum 175 where s is smaller than u include (75, 100), (80, 95), (85, 90), and (87, 88), and s can be anything from 75 to 87.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.prompt: Briefly explain to Hajun why (70 + 90) ÷ 2 = 80 cannot be the average of the six tests.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many scores the 70 points evens out.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.1: If 70 points and 90 points are each counted just once in the same way, compare how many tests each score ends up standing for.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does it show that the 70 points is not one score but a value that evens out the scores of five tests?
y-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say where the new average would fall between 70 and 90 according to your explanation (whether closer to 70)?
y-m-15-02.s.s3.model.0: The 70 points is the average of 5 tests, so the sum of the 5 tests is 350 points. If you add 90 points to that you get 440 points, and you have to divide by 6. If you just divide the two numbers by 2, you count the first 5 tests as if they were one.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.model.1: The 70 points is a value made up of five tests, and the 90 points is just one test. But the 80 points, which counts both once each, reflects far too little of the first five tests. So it should be closer to 70 than to 80.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: I explained it by the difference in share (weight) without using sums.

y-m-15-03.title: If you draw a blank and set it aside, what happens to the next person's chance?
y-m-15-03.topic: Chance (when the drawn slip is put back and when it is not)
y-m-15-03.goal: In a situation where the number of slips in the box changes, compare and revise the size of the chance according to newly learned facts, and tell the difference between putting back and not putting back.
y-m-15-03.material: A box holds 10 slips of the same shape and size. Of these, 2 slips are 'winner' and 8 are 'blank'. After shaking the box to mix them well, people take turns, closing their eyes, drawing one slip and opening it. Everyone can see the result of the drawn slip. Below, the inside of the box changes at each step.
y-m-15-03.thinking.0: Revising the chance using newly learned information
y-m-15-03.thinking.1: Comparing sizes by considering the total number and the number of winners together
y-m-15-03.thinking.2: Telling apart results that depend on a condition (whether it is put back)
y-m-15-03.prereq.0: Saying chance as the size of 'a part of the whole'; comparing the sizes of fractions (5th-grade level)
y-m-15-03.prereq.1: Chance words: impossible, even chance, certain
y-m-15-03.s.s1.prompt: New information is revealed at each step. Each time, choose how you think about the chance.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first count how many slips are in the box now and how many of them are winners.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.1: Put the picture of the box from the previous step beside the picture of the box now, and find what has changed.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Jiu is about to draw a slip first. The box has 10 slips and 2 are winners.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the right way to describe the chance that Jiu draws a winning slip?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.after: 2 of 10 slips are winners, so it is 1/5 of the whole. It is right to say it is lower than an even chance (1/2) and not impossible (0). Also, 'about one time in five' only describes the size of the chance and does not mean that one of five draws will surely be a winner.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: There are only 2 winners, so Jiu, who draws first, cannot win
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A low chance and an impossible event are different. The winning slips are in the box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There are fewer winners than blanks, so it is lower than an even chance but not impossible
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You compared the numbers of winners and blanks to describe the size of the chance. You placed it well between impossible and certain.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is 2 of 10, so the chance is roughly one time in five
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You expressed the chance as the size of a part of the whole (2/10). It means the same as saying it is low.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The person who draws first has the biggest advantage, so the chance of winning is high
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The order alone does not fix the chance. First consider the number of winners and the total number in the box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.info: The slip Jiu drew was a blank. Jiu did not put that slip back in the box. Now Harin is about to draw.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How would you say the chance that Harin draws a winning slip compares with the chance Jiu had before drawing?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.after: At first it was 2 of 10, but one blank has gone, so it is 2 of 9. 2/9 is a little bigger than 2/10. The chance changed because we know Jiu's result.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The winners are still 2 and the total is 9, so it went up a little
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You reconsidered both the number of winners and the total. You saw that one blank leaving changes the chance.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Jiu took away a blank, so it is now the turn for a winner to come out, and the chance went up
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The reason is not a 'turn' but that the number in the box changed. Explain it using what is in the box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: We can't know yet. Mixing the slips is luck, so the chance can't be known either
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Even if it is luck, you can state the size of the chance from the numbers in the box. Count the winners and the total remaining.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Only one slip is gone, so the chance stays the same
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The total went down but the number of winners stayed the same. Write them as fractions and compare.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Harin also drew a blank. This time Harin put that slip back into the box and mixed well. Now Doyun is about to draw. Jiu's blank is still outside the box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would you say the chance that Doyun draws a winning slip compares with the chance just before Harin drew?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Harin put back the blank that was drawn, so the box has the same 9 slips (2 winners) as just before Harin drew. The chance stays 2/9. If it had not been put back, it would have been 2 of 8, which would be higher.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Another blank came out, so it went up compared with before Harin drew
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Harin put the blank back. Count for yourself whether the number in the box went down.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is the same as when there were 10 slips at the start. Harin put the blank back, so everything went back to the start
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Harin's blank came back, but Jiu's blank is still outside. Count the number of slips in the box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Harin has drawn too, so it went down
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: If it is put back, the box is the same as before Harin drew. Look at what is in the box, not at how many people have drawn.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is the same as just before Harin drew. The box still has 9 slips and 2 of them are winners
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You counted the number of slips in the box yourself and compared. You pointed out that when a slip is put back, the box looks the same as before.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.reflect: How did the chance you first thought of change, or stay the same, at each step? Which information changed the chance, and which information did not?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain, using numbers of slips, how the next person's chance differs when the drawn blank is not put back and when it is put back.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of slips in the box when one blank is kept outside the box and when it is put back.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the number of winning slips is the same or different in the two cases.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If it is not put back, ...
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: When it is not put back, did you write which changed, the total number of slips or the number of winners?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: For the case where it is put back, did you write what the box looks like?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it clear whether the chance you wrote became bigger than at the start (2/10) or stayed the same?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.model.0: If it is not put back, one blank is gone, so 9 slips are left in the box and the winners stay at 2, so the chance goes up a little. If it is put back, the number of slips stays the same, so the chance does not change.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.model.1: If you put the blank you took out back in, the box goes back to how it was, so it stays 2/10. If you don't put it back, it changes to 2/9 and goes up a little.

y-m-15-04.title: What can we say for sure from the numbers in the table alone?
y-m-15-04.topic: Reading a table: what can be stated and what cannot be known from multiple-response data
y-m-15-04.goal: In a survey table where one person can choose several items, sort out what can be said for sure and what you need to know more, and make different records that match the same table.
y-m-15-04.material:
24 students in one 5th-grade class answered a survey that said, ‘Choose all the sports you like.’ They could choose all that they liked from soccer and basketball, and they were also allowed to choose none. All 24 students handed in the survey.

| Sport | Number of students who chose it |
| Soccer | 14 students |
| Basketball | 11 students |
y-m-15-04.thinking.0: Sorting statements that the data settles from those it does not settle
y-m-15-04.thinking.1: Explaining why the information is not enough using the overlap (students who chose both)
y-m-15-04.thinking.2: Making different cases that make up the same table
y-m-15-04.prereq.0: Reading a table; sums and differences of numbers (5th-grade level)
y-m-15-04.prereq.1: Meaning of statements that contain 'at least' and 'all'
y-m-15-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements that you can say must be right from this table and the description above alone.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, check 'is it always so if I use only the numbers in the table?' Imagine one case where it is not always so.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.hint.1: Add 14 and 11 and compare whether it is greater or less than the number of students in the class.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.a: There is a student who chose neither soccer nor basketball
y-m-15-04.s.s1.r.a: This cannot be known from the table. Depending on how many students chose both, there may or may not be such a student.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.b: The number of students who did not choose soccer is 10
y-m-15-04.s.s1.r.b: This is a certain statement, using the condition that all 24 handed in together with the number 14.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.c: The number of students who chose only soccer is 14
y-m-15-04.s.s1.r.c: Among the 14 who chose soccer, some may have chosen basketball too. This statement is not right.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.d: There is at least one student who chose both soccer and basketball
y-m-15-04.s.s1.r.d: You checked the overlap using the fact that adding the two numbers gives more than 24 students.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.e: The number of students who chose basketball is less than half of the class
y-m-15-04.s.s1.r.e: 11 is less than half of 24 (12 students), so this is a certain statement.
y-m-15-04.s.s1.explain: b is certain because 24-14=10. For d, 14+11=25 is greater than 24, so there must be at least 1 student who overlaps. e is certain because 11 is less than 12. a cannot be known unless you know the number of students who chose both, and c is not 14 because there are students who chose both.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different class records that match the table above exactly. x is the number of students who chose both soccer and basketball, and y is the number of students who chose neither.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the number of students x who chose both first, and write how many chose only soccer and how many chose only basketball.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.hint.1: Fit y so that the four parts (soccer only, basketball only, both, neither) add up to 24 students.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of students are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of students must be natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The number who chose both is not more than the number who chose basketball (11 students).
y-m-15-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of students who chose both cannot be more than the 11 who chose basketball.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Soccer only, basketball only, both, and neither add up to 24 students.
y-m-15-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Check that adding all four parts gives 24 students. (soccer only = 14-x, basketball only = 11-x)
y-m-15-04.s.s2.explain: Soccer only 14-x students, basketball only 11-x students, both x students, and neither y students must add up to 24 students. Then y is 1 less than x, so (1, 0), (2, 1), (5, 4), (11, 10), and so on are possible. Even for the same table there are many records, so if you don't know how many chose both, you can't tell whether there are students who chose neither.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.prompt: To say for sure whether ‘there is a student who chose neither soccer nor basketball’ is right, what more would you need to know from the survey? Write it with a reason.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare a record you made where y is 0 with one where it is not 0, and find which values differ between the two records.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether knowing that different value would let you know y too.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. What we need to know more is ...
y-m-15-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If you learn the ‘more you need to know’ that you wrote, will it be settled for sure whether the statement is right?
y-m-15-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason why the two numbers in the table (14, 11) alone are not enough?
y-m-15-04.s.s3.model.0: We need to know how many students chose both. Then we can find the number of students who chose at least one of soccer or basketball and compare it with 24 students.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.model.1: We have to ask directly whether there are students who chose nothing. Or we have to find out the number of students who chose both sports. This is because if we look only at the table, the records come out in many ways.
y-m-15-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: I mentioned both the way of finding the overlap and the way of checking directly.

y-m-15-05.title: If we find out what 100 students think by asking 20 students
y-m-15-05.topic: Collecting data: comparing ways to choose who to survey
y-m-15-05.goal: Compare several ways of choosing a part when surveying everyone is hard, make your own plan that divides the number of people so the result does not lean to one side, and also state its limits.
y-m-15-05.material: The 5th grade has Class 1 with 28 students, Class 2 with 26, Class 3 with 24, and Class 4 with 22, 100 students in all. The student council wants to find out ‘the activity students most want to do during break time.’ There is not enough time to ask all 100 students separately, so they want to ask only 20 students. You have to decide how to choose the 20 students from the methods below.
y-m-15-05.thinking.0: Comparing and evaluating whether a survey method leans to one side
y-m-15-05.thinking.1: Making several plans within the conditions
y-m-15-05.thinking.2: Stating both the strengths and the limits of a method
y-m-15-05.prereq.0: Experience showing data with tables and bar graphs (4th–5th grade level)
y-m-15-05.prereq.1: Dividing by estimating numbers: about 1 in 5
y-m-15-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the method that best lets you find out what the 100 fifth graders think from the answers of 20 students.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, check ‘are there students who cannot be chosen?’ Find which students can never be chosen.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare what difference arises if you choose the same number from classes with different numbers of students, like Class 1 and Class 4.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.a: Go find 20 fifth graders who are out on the playground during break time and ask them
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.a: Students who come out to the playground may already lean to one side in their choice of activity. Students who are in the classroom can never be chosen.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.b: Pick one class and ask 20 students in that class
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.b: One class's thinking may differ from the other classes. The students in the other classes have no chance of being chosen at all.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.c: Ask 20 students, those with attendance numbers 1 to 5 in each class
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.c: Who gets chosen is already fixed by the numbers, so the other students have no chance of being chosen, and since it is the same 5 in every class, it also cannot reflect the difference in the number of students.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.d: In each class, mix the numbers and draw, but set the number of students drawn from each class to match the size of the class
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.d: Everyone has a chance of being chosen, and the class sizes are reflected too. It used two ideas for reducing leaning together.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.e: Hand out a short questionnaire to all 100 fifth graders and collect and tally them
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.e: This is the idea of including every student's thinking. It takes more time and effort, and you need to consider that some students may not hand it in.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.explain: To avoid leaning to one side, every student should have a chance of being chosen, and it is better to reflect class size too. So drawing at random in each class, with the number from each class set to match the number of students, is the suitable method. Getting a questionnaire from all 100 students can also be used, but it has limits under the condition that time is short.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.acc.0: If the questionnaire is short, collecting it from all 100 students is also one method. But under the condition that time is short, you should compare it with the method of choosing just 20 students, and state the limit that some students may not hand in the questionnaire.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different plans for how many students to choose from each class for the 20 students. Take it as choosing about 1 in 5 students, and the number chosen from each class must not differ by more than 1 student from (number of students in the class ÷ 5). The total is 20 students. (Class 1 a, Class 2 b, Class 3 c, Class 4 d)
y-m-15-05.s.s2.hint.0: First find each class's number of students divided by 5, and find which whole numbers are within 1 student of it.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write down the possible numbers for each class, then find the combinations in which the four numbers add up to 20.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.var.a: Number to choose from Class 1 (28 students)
y-m-15-05.s.s2.var.b: Number to choose from Class 2 (26 students)
y-m-15-05.s.s2.var.c: Number to choose from Class 3 (24 students)
y-m-15-05.s.s2.var.d: Number to choose from Class 4 (22 students)
y-m-15-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of students to choose are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of students to choose must be natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of students from the four classes do not add up to 20.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The Class 1 number is within 1 student of 28÷5.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Class 1 must be set close to 28÷5 (within 1 student).
y-m-15-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The Class 2 number is within 1 student of 26÷5.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c4: Class 2 must be set close to 26÷5 (within 1 student).
y-m-15-05.s.s2.ok.c5: The Class 3 number is within 1 student of 24÷5.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c5: Class 3 must be set close to 24÷5 (within 1 student).
y-m-15-05.s.s2.ok.c6: The Class 4 number is within 1 student of 22÷5.
y-m-15-05.s.s2.fail.c6: Class 4 must be set close to 22÷5 (within 1 student).
y-m-15-05.s.s2.explain: 28÷5=5.6, 26÷5=5.2, 24÷5=4.8, and 22÷5=4.4. So Class 1 is 5 to 6 students, Class 2 is 5 to 6, Class 3 is 4 to 5, and Class 4 is 4 to 5, and there are six plans in all that add up to 20 students. e.g. (5, 5, 5, 5), (6, 5, 5, 4), (6, 6, 4, 4).
y-m-15-05.s.s3.prompt: Write one reason why the method you chose (or the plan you made above) is good for showing what the whole 5th grade thinks, and one limit that still remains.
y-m-15-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write whether there are students who cannot be chosen in your method.
y-m-15-05.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine one situation in which the result from the 20 students and the result from all 100 students could differ.
y-m-15-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether there are students in your method who have no chance of being chosen?
y-m-15-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write why the result from 20 students could differ from all 100?
y-m-15-05.s.s3.model.0: If you draw numbers at random in each class, matched to the number of students, every student has a chance of being chosen, so it does not lean to one side. Still, we asked only 20 students, so the result could differ from asking all 100.
y-m-15-05.s.s3.model.1: I chose the method of handing out a questionnaire to all 100 students. It can include every student's thinking, so it shows the whole well. But if some students don't hand in the questionnaire, there is a limit that their thinking is left out.
y-m-15-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: Even if you choose another method, you wrote the reason and the limit together.

y-m-15-06.title: In the box with the most red, is red the most likely to come out?
y-m-15-06.topic: Comparing chances: having more of something versus having a bigger chance
y-m-15-06.goal: When comparing boxes of marbles, confirm and explain with a counterexample that you must compare the share that red takes up of the whole, not just the number of red marbles.
y-m-15-06.material:
There are three boxes holding marbles that are all the same size and shape. From each box you will close your eyes and take out one marble. Every marble is either red or blue.

| Box | Total marbles | Red marbles |
| 가 | 5 | 4 |
| 나 | 10 | 7 |
| 다 | 8 | 5 |

Yuna said, “Box 나 has the most red marbles, 7, so red is the most likely to come out of Box 나.”
y-m-15-06.thinking.0: Evaluating a friend's judgment using evidence
y-m-15-06.thinking.1: Making a counterexample where there are more but the chance is lower
y-m-15-06.thinking.2: Explaining the standard for comparison (the share) in words
y-m-15-06.prereq.0: Writing a part of the whole as a fraction; comparing the sizes of fractions (5th-grade level)
y-m-15-06.prereq.1: The meaning of taking one out with your eyes closed: every marble has an equal chance of being picked
y-m-15-06.s.s1.prompt: Which of the three boxes has the highest chance of a red marble coming out?
y-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each box, write ‘how many of the whole marbles are red’ as a fraction in the same form.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.1: Change the fractions to decimals or make the denominators the same, and compare their sizes.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.a: Box 나 (because it has the most red, 7)
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.a: You only looked at the red count being the largest. The total number of marbles differs between boxes. Compare the share that red takes up of the whole.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.b: Box 가 (because red takes up the largest share of the whole marbles)
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.b: You judged not by the count but by the share compared with the whole. Even if the boxes differ in size, they can be compared by the same standard.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.c: Box 다 (because it has the fewest blue mixed in, 3)
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.c: You only looked at the number of blue. Even if there is little blue, if the total is small, red's share changes.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.d: All three boxes are the same (because all the boxes contain red)
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.d: Just containing red does not let you compare the sizes of the chances.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.explain: The chance of red coming out is compared by the share of red in the whole. Box 가 has 4 of 5, so 4/5=0.8; Box 나 has 7/10=0.7; Box 다 has 5/8=0.625. So Box 가 is the highest.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different cases where ‘the box with more red also has the higher chance of red coming out’ is wrong. The first box is r1/t1 (r1 red out of t1 total marbles) and the second box is r2/t2. The first box has more red, but its chance of red must be lower. The total marbles are 20 or fewer, and the first box must have at least 1 blue.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make the total of the first box large and make its red number only a little bigger than the second box's.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write each box's share of red as a decimal and check that the first is smaller.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of marbles are natural numbers and 20 or fewer.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of marbles must be natural numbers, and each box's total must be 20 or fewer. The second box must also have at least 1 red.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c2: Red does not exceed the total, and the first box has blue too.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Red cannot be more than the total, and the first box must have at least 1 blue.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The first box has more red.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of red in the first box must be greater than in the second box.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c4: The chance of red coming out of the first box is lower.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c4: r1/t1 of the first box must be smaller than r2/t2 of the second box. Compare the two shares.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.explain: For example, if the first box has 7 red of 10 (0.7) and the second box has 4 red of 5 (0.8), the first box has more red but a lower chance. 6/15=0.4 and 4/5=0.8, 5/12 and 2/3, and 9/20 and 5/8 work too.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Yuna what should be compared when comparing chances, using the example you made above or the numbers for Box 가 and Box 나.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.hint.0: First say in words which of Box 가 and Box 나 makes red easier to come out, then support the reason with numbers.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.hint.1: Also think about what you may compare if two boxes have the same total number of marbles.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. You shouldn't look only at the number of red. Because ...
y-m-15-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the example I gave, can you see in numbers which box has the higher chance?
y-m-15-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the idea of ‘comparing with the whole’ in my explanation?
y-m-15-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about when having more red means the same as having a bigger chance? (When the totals are the same)
y-m-15-06.s.s3.model.0: You shouldn't look only at the number of red. Box 가 has 4 of 5, so red is more likely to come out than from Box 나, which has 7 of 10. You have to compare the share that red takes up of all the marbles.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.model.1: Having more doesn't mean a bigger chance. 4/5=0.8 and 7/10=0.7, so Box 가 is higher. You have to compare by the ratio, and you can compare just the counts only when the totals are the same.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: I even mentioned the case where comparing just the counts is fine (when the totals are the same).

y-m-15-07.title: Why do bars look different in length for the same scores?
y-m-15-07.topic: Reading bar graphs: where the scale starts and the impression of bar length
y-m-15-07.goal: Know that bar lengths for the same data look different depending on the value at which the vertical scale starts, find and fix a reading that causes a misunderstanding, and write a title that informs without causing a misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.material:
The unit-test average of Class 1 in the 5th grade is 82 points, and the average of Class 2 is 85 points. You drew the same data in two bar graphs for the class newspaper. All the bars go from the bottom upward.
- Graph ㉮: The vertical scale starts at 0 points and goes up to 100 points, with 10 points per division.
- Graph ㉯: The vertical scale starts at 80 points and goes up to 90 points, with 1 point per division. The part below 80 points is not drawn, and the bars show only the part that rises above 80 points.

Doun looked at graph ㉯ and explained as below.
y-m-15-07.thinking.0: Finding the error in reading a graph
y-m-15-07.thinking.1: Evaluating what action is needed when the graph is printed as it is
y-m-15-07.thinking.2: Rewriting a title with the reader in mind
y-m-15-07.prereq.0: Reading the vertical scale and bar height of a bar graph (4th-grade level)
y-m-15-07.prereq.1: Comparing how many times one number is another (relation between multiplication and division)
y-m-15-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that is wrong in Doun's explanation. (Count the lines starting from 1.)
y-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.0: Explain in words, without a picture, whether the part of the bars in graph ㉯ below 80 points can be seen.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.1: Put Class 2's score and Class 1's score side by side and estimate how many times one score is the other.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.0: In graph ㉯, the vertical scale starts at 80 points, with 1 point per division.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.1: The Class 1 bar is drawn 82-80=2 divisions high, and the Class 2 bar is 85-80=5 divisions high.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.2: 5 divisions is 2.5 times 2 divisions, so Class 2's score is 2.5 times Class 1's score.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.3: In graph ㉮, the difference in the lengths of the two bars looks very small compared with the bar heights.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. In graph ㉯ the bar length shows only the part that rises above 80 points, so the ratio of 5 divisions to 2 divisions (2.5 times) is not the ratio of the scores. Comparing the scores 85 and 82 gives about 1.04 times, which is almost the same. Line 4 is right. In graph ㉮, which starts from 0 points, the two bars look almost the same length.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.prompt: You want to print graph ㉯ in the newspaper. Choose all the suitable ways to keep the friends who read it from misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each choice, consider ‘does it make it more likely or less likely that a reader friend will judge by bar length alone?’
y-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find which method lets people know the real difference between the scores 82 and 85.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.a: Write in words that the vertical scale starts at 80 points, or put a break mark below the scale
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.a: Telling where the scale starts helps readers not to read bar length as the score itself.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.b: Color only the Class 2 bar a dark color so it stands out
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.b: Using a different color makes the impression of the length even stronger. It is not a way to reduce misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.c: Switch to printing graph ㉮, whose scale starts at 0 points
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.c: If the starting value of the scale is set to 0, the ratio of the bar lengths gets close to the ratio of the scores.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.d: Write the graph's title as ‘Class 2 is 2.5 times higher than Class 1’
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.d: This is a statement that wrongly reads the ratio of bar lengths as the ratio of scores.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.e: Write the numbers 82 points and 85 points on the bars as well
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.e: Showing the numbers together lets readers read the values directly instead of judging only by the impression of length.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.explain: Telling the starting value of the scale (a), changing it to start from 0 (c), and writing the numbers together (e) all reduce misunderstanding caused by bar length. A dark color (b) or a title like ‘2.5 times’ (d) makes the misunderstanding bigger.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.acc.0: Printing graph ㉯ as it is while also telling the scale's starting value and the scores is also a suitable way to reduce misunderstanding. It is even better combined with changing to a graph that starts from 0.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.acc.1: Changing the scale to 0 and writing the scores together is also a suitable way.
y-m-15-07.s.s3.prompt: Write a new one-line news title for the class newspaper. It must report the scores of Class 1 and Class 2 just as they are, without causing a misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.s.s3.hint.0: Use 82 and 85 as they are, and add one more thing: how many points the difference between the two scores is.
y-m-15-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how a friend who doesn't know the scale would take the difference in scores when reading your finished title.
y-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: From the title alone, can you see that the difference between 82 and 85 points is not big?
y-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the scores directly, so that even a friend who hasn't seen the graph won't misunderstand?
y-m-15-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you tell apart ‘higher’ and ‘much higher’?
y-m-15-07.s.s3.model.0: Class 1 averages 82 points and Class 2 averages 85 points, a 3-point difference
y-m-15-07.s.s3.model.1: Class 2 is 3 points higher than Class 1 (the graph scale starts at 80 points)
y-m-15-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: I told the difference and even where the scale starts.
y-m-15-07.s.s3.model.2: Class 1 got 82 points and Class 2 got 85 points, so the two classes' scores are similar
y-m-15-07.s.s3.modelNote.2: I wrote the numbers together with the judgment ‘similar’. The reader decides whether the word ‘similar’ is suitable.
